speechtext:
Air. Speaker, I wish to speak to a question of privilege 4. few evenings ago, when I had the honour of addressing the House on the surrender of St. Peter's Reserve, I stated that, an account had been rendered by one E. Rayner, who claimed that, his work was to have cost something like $500, and when the account was rendered to the Department of Indian Affairs, the department refused to pay it. I pointed put that this money had been paid, and I su^-gested that the extra land that- had been given to the chief and councillors had been used for that purpose. This was the only part of the serious charges which I brought before the House against the department that the hon. Alinister of the Interior, in his three hours speech replying to me, attempted to refute. In that "attempt, he denied the accuracy of my statement in regard to the extra land which the chief and the councillors had received, and in doing so quoted what I understood him to say were the official figures from his department, and he asked the House to accept them rather than the statement made bv myself. The facts, AH. Speaker, which I intend to lay before the House are shown by a sworn return of J. 0. Lewis, an Indian agent at Selkirk, which I have here of the payments to the)Indians of the $5,000 which

the deputy superintendent general of Indian Affairs, Mr. Pedley, had promised them if they voted for the surrender. This return gives the names of each man of the band and the number of his children and the amounts the different Indians received of this $5,000. So that there can be no doubt that each family was fully represented under the head of such family, and ttie head of such families was there to make the familv look as large and numerous as possible,' so that his share of the $5,000 would be as great as possible. This I am sure will not be questioned by any lion, member of this House. Then Mr. Speaker, this pay roll which I hold in my hand shows beyond any doubt the number of children each councillor and the chief had. I will now read to the House the headings under which the members of the family are accounted for. I will also read the declaration attached to this pay roll. I have, Mr. Speaker, in my hands the pay roll for the distribution of the $5,000 that Mr. Pedley took to St. Peter's Indian reserve and distributed among the Indians _ after they agreed to the surrender and it is headed in this way:
Treaty No. 1. St. Peter's Band, paid at St. Peter's Reserve, September 23, 1907. Land Fund.
The different headings follow. It is made out in regular form showing how many men, women and children there were. It starts with men, women, boys, girls, males and females. We will take just one of these men in question. We will take the chief, Wm. Prince. According to this sworn return we find that he had just himself and his wife. He received $18.60 out of that fund. That money was paid by Mr. Pedley himself according to the book. Wm. Henry Prince according to this sworn return had two of a family, and got $14.60 and that was paid by Mr. Pedley. Each of the councillors received their money directly from the hands of Mr. Pedley. Now what I rose in my place this morning to correct was the statement made by the hon. minister denying my statement that the chief and the councillors had received more lands than they were legally entitled to under the surrender. The hon. gentleman denied that fact and he says, and I am quoting from ( Hansard of the 14th:
My hon. friend explained that Mr. Rayner had got back the extra money that he had paid to the Indians, because the chiefs had got a certain proportion more land than they were entitled to under the terms of the surrender. That is to say that Chief William Prince got 20 acres more, and the several councillors a certain number of acres more, in the neighbourhood of 20 apiece over and above what the terms of surrender called for. Chief Wiliam Prince was entitled to 212 acres by reason of his extra allowance as chief, and bv reason of the number of members in
liis family, and he received actually 215.53, that is 31 acres more than his allowance. Councillor Harper was entitled to 232 acres, and he got 233-16. Councillor James was entitled to 200 acres, and he got 206 -88. Councillor Henry Prince was entitled to 168 acres, and he got 172-50. John Prince was entitled to 136 acres, and he got 136 acres. The explanation is that in the laying out of the lands when the survey was made, the lots ran into one or two acres more than the allowance called for, and the block was allowed to go as it was surveyed. My hon. friend stated last night that these people received in the neighbourhood of 20 acres at least more than they were entitled to, and that this_ extra allowance of land was in some way, which he did not explain, used to repay Rayner the money that he said it was rumoured had been paid to the Indians.

Sir WILFRID LAL'RIER moved the third reading of Bill (No. 95) respecting the Naval Service of Canada. He said: I promised my hon. friend the leader of the opposition yesterday to give him some information. which I now present to the House.

I have expressed my views at considerable length on two occasions with regard to the measure that is now before us for the third reading; for that reason it will not be necessary for me to inflict upon the House any lengthy remarks at the present moment. I do not intend to go over matters that I have already debated; there are, however, one or two considerations which I feel it my duty to present to the House before the third reading is passed. I have not found an absolute wealth of information available with regard to the details of this measure. Yesterday I put a number of questions to the government which, owing to some confusion in the arrangement of their documents, they were not able to answer at the moment. I cannot see that the memorandum which I have received from the Prime Minister this morning is very illuminating, as it consists for the most part of a reference to matters that have already been set forth on the pages of ' Hansard.' In fact, so far as the details of the measure are concerned, I would be inclined to think that the government are wandering in a sort of Serbonian bog in which there is not much light respecting the proposals that are before the House.
Now the problem of co-operation in the defence of the empire is undoubtedly a very grave one. Two considerations present themselves immediately when that question is before us. The first consideration is how we may best give aid in what I consider to be the present emergent condition of the empire; the second is what will be a reasonable basis of permanent cooperation by Canada in the naval defence of the empire. So far as I am concerned.
I have endeavoured to keep those questions absolutely distinct, as I think they are distinct in themselves. Ever since we first discussed this question on the floor of the House in the month of March, 1909, it. has seemed to me that an immediate and effective aid to the empire in the present emerg-

ent conditions can only be accomplished, or at least can best be accomplished, by placing a certain sum of money at the disposal of the imperial ^authorities of Great Britain as represented by the admiralty, and inviting them to make the best disposal of that money, in their judgment, for the purpose of increasing the united naval strength of the empire I have set out my views on that matter in the resolution which I moved in this House on the second reading, and I need not repeat my observations thereon. I shall come to one or two details of the government measure in a moment. I desire to say at this juncture that I regard the subject of permanent co-operation by Canada in the naval defence of the empire as one that should be properly submitted to the people of this country before any plan of permanent co-operation is entered upon by Canada. Some very strong criticism of our position in that regard has been made by the Prime Minister, by the Minister -of Militia and Defence and by other hon. gentlemen opposite. 1 have not observed anything in those criticisms which alters the opinion I have expressed. If I were inclined, I could quote this morning from speeches made in the past by the Prime Minister himself upon the proposal to build the Canadian Pacific railway, from speeches made by the Minister of Militia and Defence himself upon that proposal and upon other proposals; I could quote the remarks hnd the votes of those hon. gentlemen in this House, who, in respect of matters that had 'been canvassed in this country for years, declared that measures should not pass parliament until the actual proposals had passed through the ordeal of a general election, that they should only be passed by a parliament that came back with a mandate from the people in that regard. For example, although the proposal to build the Canadian Pacific railway had been before this country for no less than 8 years, and had been discussed upon every platform in the country, both of these hon. gentlemen voted in this House for a resolution which declared, 'that the contract should not be ratified till after the people had had _ the opportunity of expressing their opinion through the medium of a general election.' As neither the Prime Minister nor the Minister of Militia said a single word in support of that motion they must be regarded as concurring in the arguments used by one of their supporters at that time, who made the motion on their behalf.
Was not that expression of opinion given in face of the fact that a much more favourable offer to build that railway had been made by another company?

The hon. gentleman may be correct or not correct in that re-

The point of my contention is that he declared ' that the contract should not be ratified till after the people had had an opportunity of expressing their opinion through the. medium of a general election.' That parliament had been elected to a certain extent on that issue, and I will invite my hon. friend to consider the reasons to which he committed himself for his silent vote. Mr. Bechard, who made that motion, speaking for his colleagues, used the following language:
'I contend this whole subject should be laid before the people for their decision at the polls. The ground on which I base my contention is that in a question of such great consequence for the weel or woe of the country, the people should have an opportunity of pronouncing on this new policy and scheme submitted by the government. True this Pacifio Railway question has been before the people for years, and that it has been the settled policy Qf the country to build a road connecting the eastern with the western provinces, and that this road should be continued to the Pacific coast; but it is equally true that the policy now before us to attain that end is completely new to the people. . . .
'We do not know what is the real sentiment of the people at present with reference to this scheme. . . .
* I believe it is difficult for any of us to say what is the real sentiment of the people with regard to the question, and I think that the only way of ascertaining it would be an appeal to the judgment of the people.'
I say that every one of these considerations is an infinitely stronger consideration why the mandate of the people should be sought at a general election on the present occasion than it was when the Prime Minister and the Minister of Militia voted for that particualr motion in 1881. This proposal has not been before the people at all. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister cannot deny that. What was his attitude in 1907 at the imperial conference? His attitude-and upon that attitude he went to the country in 1908 -was exactly the reverse of the policy he has presented to the House in this Bill. He declared at the imperial conference of 1907, in language which has been quoted over and over again in this House, in language as explicit and forcible as it would be possible for any man to use, that he would have absolutely none of the policy that he is presenting to the House today. So I say as far as our position is concerned in seeking the mandate _ of the people at a general election with regard to a basis of permanent co-operation for the defence of the empire, we had nothing to retract. We stand, as we have always stood in that respect, on two considerations-first, that the emergent conditions of the empire do demand immediate and effective aid, and, in the second place, that before a basis of permanent cooperation in the naval defence of the em-

pire is entered upon, the people of this country have a right to be consulted and to give their mandate.
A great deal has been said about the resolution of March, 1909, and at the risk of wearying the House I wish to say one or two words in that connection. It has been charged over and over again by hon. gentlemen on the othfer side of the House that the Conservative party in opposing this Bill, is departing in some way from the terms of that resolution. I desire to challenge that statement as directly as it can be challenged in parliamentary language. I say that those who have departed from the resolution of 1909 are the hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches. Can there be any doubt upon that? Let me invite once more the attention of the House to the following clause which was contained ill that resolution:
The House will eordiallv approve of any necessary expenditure designed to promote the speedy organization of a Canadian naval service in co-operation with and in close relation to the imperial navy, along the lines suggested by the admiralty at the last imperial conference, and in full sympathy with the view that the naval supremacy of Britain is essential to the security of commerce, the safety of the empire and the peace of the world.
In order to ascertain whether or not the proposals of the government follow the resolution of March, 1909, it is necessary in the first place to ascertain whether those proposals are along the lines suggested by the admiralty at the last imperial conference, that is, the conference of 1907. Those lines were laid down and declared in the clearest- possible terms by Lord Tweed-mouth, at that time the First Lord of the Admiralty. This is what he said:
The -only reservation that the admiralty desire to make is that they claim to have the charge of the stragetical questions which are necessarily involved in naval defence, to hold the command of the naval forces of the country, and to arrange the distribution of ships in the best possible manner, to resist attacks and to defend the empire at large whether it be our own islands or the dominions beyond the seas.
We thoroughly recognize that we are responsible for that defence. We want yon to help us ill that defence. We want vou to give us all the assistance you can, but' we do not come to you as beggars ; we gladly take all that you can give us, but at the same time, if you are not inclined to give us the help that we hope to have from you, we acknowledge our absolute obligation to defend the ivmg s dominions across the seas to the best of our ability.
No question there, as to whether the emergency in question affects the British isles or not, no question there of going to the help of any of the Dominions beyond the seas provided the war is just

or provided the interests of the British empire as a whole are concerned, but a broad, loyal, generous declaration that whatever may be the emergency the mother country will gladly come to the aid of the Dominions beyond the seas.
What is the reservation which Lord Tweedmouth claimed in that statement?
The only reservation that the admiralty desire to make is, that they claim to have charge of these strategical questions whicn are necessarily involved in naval defence, to hold the command of the naval forces of the country, and to arrange the distribution of ships in the best possible manner to resist attack and to defend the empire at large, whether it be our own islands or the dominions beyond the seas.
How is that carried out by the proposals of the government? Can any/ man, taking a reasonable view of this Bill say that it is on the lines suggested by Lord Tweedmouth in the quotations I have just read?
I have here section 18 of the Bill. The section provides:
In the case of an emergency the Governor in Council may place at the disposal of His Majesty, for general service in the Royal navy, the naval service or any part thereof, any ships or vessels of the naval service, and the officers and seamen serving in such ships or vessels, or any officers or seamen belonging to the naval service.
What is the meaning of that proposal? The Prime Minister has set forth its meaning in the debate in committee. I shall not attempt to give the committee the whole of his observations, but I shall read one passage which I think ought to be placed before the House in connection with the quotation I have already made. On page 7626 of the unrevised 'Hansard1 I find:

Would the right hon. gentleman permit me to ask him a question? Suppose a Canadian ship meets a ship of similar armament and power belonging to an enemy, meets her on the high seas, what is she to do? 1 do not ask now what she will do if attacked, but will she attack, will she tight ?
Sir I\ ILFRID LAITRIER. I do not know that she would fight. I do not know that she isliould fight either. She should not fight until the government by which she is commissioned have determined whether she should go into the war. That is the position we _ take, my hon. friend takes a different position. He says that without any question, under all circumstances, we are bound to send our ships into the war. We take a different position, and we say: Let the country judge between us.
Would our ports and harbours be neutral like our fleet until an order in council had been passed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not understand what my hon. friend means by asking if they should be neutral.

I understand the

Prime Minister to say that our ships would not fight until they were ordered to do so, and, therefore, they would in effect be neutral until the Governor in Council had made an order that they should participate in the war. Have I misstated my hon. friend's position ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No.
You e,ould not .have anything much plainer or more explicit than that.
Then, inasmuch as our ships, under the conditions mentioned, will be practically neutral, I would like to know whether our ports and harbours will also be neutral in the same way?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not understand what my hon. friend means by asking if they would remain neutral. If he means after an enemy has come into our harbour, then it will be time to resist them with our fleet.

But if our ships do not attack the enemy when they meet the enemy on the high seas, on the same principle, may not the enemy's fleet come into our harbour without resistance or attack, without any fear of aggression, surely that can be done, it is feasible for the country owning those harbours to maintain neutrality on the high seas?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That would be a question to determine any time that a warship entered a Canadian port.

The position of the Prime Minister is that ships flying the British flag should meet an enemy on the high seas and not attack them. That is a new tradition for the British navy.
I do not think there can be any misapprehension as to the position of the two parties in this connection. The Minister of Finance and other hon. gentlemen opposite have endeavoured to becloud the issue. I am not proposing that the naval forces of Canada shall be sent to every little war. Great Britain may be engaged in naval wars in which not one-tenth of her naval forces would toe called upon to act. What I contend for is the principle [DOT] that in time of war there shall be one united naval force for the whole empire and that naval force shall be available to meet any enemy that may assail the integrity of the empire. Suppose it were declared that the naval forces of Canada should be part of the naval force of the empire in time of war. It is conceivable that there might be a naval war in which Great Britain might not require or demand any assistance whatever from the naval force of this country. But there is something beyond and above all that. If the naval forces of the mother country and all the dominions form part of one great united naval force of the empire in time of war what follows? Any enemy assailing the British empire knows that it must meet those forces in time of war, that they are available for attack or resistance, for upholding the integrity of the empire and the supremacy of its 239J	J
sea control. What is the other alternative? Under the proposals of the government what may an enemy anticipate? It may anticipate that it will have to meet the naval forces of the mother country plus a potential order in council^ which may not come into force until the integrity of this empire shall have been destroyed. That, Sir, is the difference between the two proposals as it lies in my mind and I, like the Prime Minister, am ready to leave to the country to judge which proposal is truly in the interests of Canada, and in the interests of the whole empire.
The proposals of the government seem to me in one aspect to be absurd and unworkable, but in another aspect they are dangerous and revolutionary. In so far as they are not unworkable they are dangerous; in so far as they are not absurd they are revolutionary because it is absolutely inconceivable that if Great Britain were engaged in a naval war and the Canadian naval force acted as if it belonged not to the empire or to Canada but to some neutral country, such a condition would not lead or at least conduce to the early separation of this country from the British empire. I would recall some of the illustrations adduced in the debate yesterday. A Canadian ship is on the ocean, no order in council has been passed, war has been declared or an overt act committed and hostilities have actually commenced; a Canadian ship is on the high seas, flying the British flag, a cruiser of the .enemy approaches, the Canadian ship is not to attack or to fight unless she is attacked. Within sight of her, on high seas, a cruiser of the enemy may toe capturing vessels flying the British flag. Under the statement of the Prime Minister, the Canadian cruiser will not interfere because no order in council has been passed. Is such a position tenable is it. not absurd, is it not dangerous and revolutionary? Can it have any other outcome than to bring about the separation of this country from that empire whose flag flies over us to-day?
The Prime Minister seems to consider that it is possible that our ports and commerce shall also be neutral as our fleet would be under his own statement until that order in council has been passed. That would only emphasize the position I have already taken. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance says that if Great Britain became involved in any great or serious war no government in this country could live unless it sent the Canadian naval force to the assistance of the empire. Well, there are one or two considerations to be regarded in that connection. I pointed out before, and I repeat it to-day. that a delay such as that which took place at the

hands of this government in connection with the South African war might spelt disaster to the whole empire; and although condign punishment might be visited upon a government which hesitated in such an emergency, it would be small consolation to us afterwards that certain gentlemen should be driven from the treasury benches or even out of public life, when in the meantime the fate of this empire had been decided by a great naval battle in which no Canadian naval force took part. So I do not think the -question can be met in that way.
I desire further to say that if by the free act of this parliament the naval forces of Canada were placed at the disposal of the admiralty of some central authority in time of war, that would not in the least interfere with our autonomy, the danger of which has been so greatly on the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite. That course would be taken by. the free will of the people of Canada expressed through their representatives in parliament. It would, in fact, be more the act of the people of Canada than the passing of an order in council, as proposed by hon. gentlemen opposite.
I am desirous, Mr. Speaker, that this country shall co-operate upon some permanent basis in the naval defence of the empire. I do not see how it is possible for us to remain within the empire without taking some responsibility in that regard. What will the proposal of the government work out to? If we are to abstain from taking part in some war which may concern Great Britain or other dominions of the empire chiefly, will Great Britain, on the other hand, when our Pacific coast may be assailed, say that she will take no part on our behalf, and that her navy shall remain in the North Sea?
I am disposed to think that there is only one way of dealing with the naval forces of .the empire, and that is to have them united under some central control, and let the world know that those united forces are available for the maintenance of the sea supremacy of the empire in time of war. They may not be called upon when certain wars-occur, even wars involving the employment of the naval forces; but the mere fact that they are available is the important consideration. This is the principle I stand for and the principle I desire to see carried out, It is desirable, in the first place, that we should co-operate upon some permanent basis. It is desirable, in the second place, that if the conditions of the empire at the present time are emergent, we should bear some immediate and effective aid to the empire as a whole. I still maintain, notwithstanding all the arguments that have been advanced to the contrary, that the proposal I submitted to

the House involves the true principle in that regard; and that the true solution, the wise solution, of the great problem that is before the people of Canada today would be, in the first place, to bring immediate and effective aid in the manner I have already indicated to the House on the second reading of this Bill, and, in the second place, to mature more carefully and wisely the proposals for permanent co-operation by Canada in the naval defence of the empire-to bring these proposals into parliament and discuss them, then to submit them to the people at a general election, and after that to have them carried into force according to the mandate and the direction of the free people of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the exception of the few remarks I made yesterday in Committee of the Whole,, I have not yet taken any part in this discussion. Now that my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, by his speech lias reopened the whole question, I ask the permission of the House to make some observations which, perhaps, I might more fittingly have made at an earlier stage, but which, in the desire to shorten the discussion, I refrained from making. The question before us to-day is one of the greatest importance, perhaps the most important that has ever come before the parliament of this Dominion. Some may think that it involves a new principle; but if we look more closely into the matter, we shall discover that what we are doing to-day does not involve a new principle, but is merely an enlargement of a principle which the people of Canada have long accepted and had in operation. It is the history of all colonies that in their earlier stages they must look to the mother country for support; but as a colony grows in population and strength, it naturally takes upon itself some share of those responsibilities which in the earlier stage have to be assumed by the mother country. Canada has passed through that stage. In her earlier days she had to look to the mother country, as all other colonies have had to do; but as she has grown in wealth and in population she has taken upon herself those responsibilities which a self-respecting country should be ready to bear whenever she has the ability to do so. And so in the progress of time we have taken upon ourselves some share of the obligations in regard to our military defence. We had our military organizations, more or less efficient, in the various provinces before confederation, and at the time of the union there was a sort of understanding that Canada should recognize her imperial responsibilities by expending a very considerable sum for us in those days, roughly estimated at $1,000,000, for the mainten-

ance of her militia organization. From time to time progress was made in that direction until to-day we are spending some $6,000,000 or $7,000,000 a year in the maintenance of our militia system. Now, when we undertake to apply the same principle to the naval organization, the House will see on reflection, that it is not the introduction of a new principle; it is simply an extension of an old principle, an extension which we ought to make by reason of the fact that Canada is growing more rapidly in wealth, in population and in all her resources. Whatever differences there may be amongst us on matters of detail, we all recognize the fact that we belong to a world-wide empire, and that the maintenance of that empire requires a great naval force; and when the time has come that the naval organizations of other countries seem to be coming nearer to those of Great Britain, that the supremacy of Great Britain on the sea may seem to be challenged, or, if it is not challenged, the moment may not be distant when it w ill be challenged, the overseas dominions will be wise to take upon themselves some share of responsibility in naval affairs, and the only question is one of detail as to what is the best form in which that assistance can be rendered. It is too much to expect that the British islands, with their comparatively small population, shall forever bear the burdens of this great naval organization.
I accept in the fullest degree, that if we are to be citizens of this-great empire, and share in all its glory, and in all its prestige and all its power, we must be prepared to share in its responsibilities. It is a burden and we must not be too niggardly as to the amount we may be called upon to spend for such a useful, such a noble and such an imperial purpose. I want to call the attention of the House now to the question of the differences of opinion that exist between us as to the proper methods of dealing with this question. If we are all agreed that Canada must take up her share of responsibility, then we come to the consideration of the best method. Now, it is a pity that there should be differences of opinion amongst us to-day. There were none a few- months ago. I really do not think that there are good reasons for such differences of opinion. However that may be, I think we shall do well to again place on record the resolution of the House ot the 29th of March, 1909:
This House fully recognizes the duty of the people of Canada, as they increase in numbers and wealth, to assume in larger measure the responsibilities of national defence.
The House is of opinion that under the present constitutional relations between the mother country and the self-governing dominions, the payment of regular and periodical contributions to the imperial treasury for
naval and military purposes would not, eo far as Canada is concerned, be the most satisfactory solution of the question of defence.
The House will cordially approve of any necessary expenditure designed to promote the speedy organization of a Canadian naval service in co-operation with and in close relation to the imperial navy, along the lines suggested by the admiralty at the iast imperial conference, and in full sympathy with the view that the naval supremacy of Britain is essential to tile security of commerce, the safety of the empire and the peace of the world.
The House expresses its firm conviction that whenever the need arises the Canadian people will be foimd ready and willing to make any sacrifice that is required to give to the imperial authorities the most loyal and hearty co-operation in every movement for the maintenance of the integrity and honour of the empire.
I think that resolution should be quoted again and again, because I believe that on the 29th March, 1909, it correctly expressed the sentiments of the Canadian people; and now at the close or near the close of this long debate on this important measure, I . venture to read it once more and to say that the words of that resolution to-day express the deliberate judgment of the people of the Dominion of Canada. The House, in this resolution, recognized the necessity of participating in the naval movement. The House distinctly declared its conviction that the payment of a money contribution was not the most satisfactory way.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The House declared in favour of a Canadian naval service in co-operation with the imperial navy, the service which this Bill proposes to give to the empire. The House declared the readiness of the Canadian people whenever the need arises to make any sacrifice that may be necessary for the maintenance of the empire. It was the unanimous declaration of the Canadian parliament, a notice to the world of the determination of Canada to stand by the empire when a case of need should arise. We would plead to-day, if it were possible, for the same unanimity which characterized the parliament of Canada at that moment. The need of co-operation with the imperial navy is frankly recognized. We are without experience in such matters, but it is both sensible and patriotic that we should communicate with the admiralty and profit by their larger knowledge and by their greater experience, and that is exactly what we have done. The fact that we do not do all that the British government may have desired us to do, is by no means a proof that the policy we are pursuing is not entirely consistent with their views. On the contrary, so far as we are able to know, we are entirely in

harmony with the wishes of the British admiralty. We are proposing a scheme which the imperial authorities themselves laid down for our advice and our guidance.
No, no.
By no means.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Let us see what the British government asked us to do. Their first proposal was for a monetary contribution. That was the first suggested. No one doubts that that would be the most convenient form of assistance from the home point of view of the British admiralty, and it is now claimed that our government should respond to this demand. It was not so claimed in the resolution of a year ago. But, Mr. Speaker, Canada has been on record for years against monetarv contributions for naval purposes in that form. At the conference of 1902, Lord Selbome, who was then first Lord of the Admiralty, made a similar suggestion. The proposal tor a monetary contribution was emphatically rejected by the Canadian ministers attending that conference. Lord Selborne's memorandum submitted to the conference has references to contributions from the colonies, and then it says:
Sir Wilfrid Laurier informs me that His Majesty's government of the Dominion of Canada are contemplating the establishment of a local naval force in the waters of Canada, but that they were not able to make any offer of assistance analogous to those enumerated above.
. That was the declaration the Prime Minister of Canada made on behalf of the government and parliament and people of this Dominion. At a later stage, the Canadian ministers submitted a memorandum which has been read in this House before, and only a part of which I will read now:
have had discussions in parliament, from time to time on various matters of a more or less imperial character, but down to the time of the present session, down to the opening of the discussion when hon. gentlemen opposite took such a strange course at variance with their action of a year ago, the wisdom of that declaration by the Prime Minister of Canada was never called in question. We have had two general ejections since that declaration was made.
Never was heard of.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is right. They never heard of it. We have two general elections in which hon. gentlemen opposite had an opportunity to arraign this government-two appeals to the grand jury of the country. They have had these opportunities to appeal to the people and challenge the wisdom of this declaration. Now, my hon. friend from Manitoba (Mr. Schaffner) comes here to-day and confesses that in these two general elections he never heard of it.

Will the hon. Minister of Finance inform the House whether he or any of his friends or any of the government supporters ever heard it brought up?
i Mr. FIELDING. Never brought up? There never was a reason for bringing it up. It was simply consistent with the whole policy of Canada whereby we are prepared to do whatever is best to the utmost limit of our power to help the empire. But we propose to do it in our own way, consistent with the position of Canada as a daughter nation of the empire.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is all right.
^ the hon. minister (Mr. Fielding) would not mind answering another question that I think is quite relevant, I would like to ask what did the government do to inform the country as to their attitude at the conference of 1907?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
When I say it was never brought up, I mean that it was never brought up at a general election. It was brought up in the reports of the conference laid before this parliament and- s-mt to every member. It was brought up "in the 3ense that we bring up any matter bv giving the records to parliament, and inviting public discussion and critcism. The declaration of the Prime Minister of Canada was the expression of the will of the Canadian people-just as the resoultion of March 29 of last year was an expression of the will of the Canadian people; the only difference between us and hon. gentlemen opposite on

that point being that we have stood to our guns while these hon. members have not stood to their guns. I say, Sir, that, with that record of the conference before the country for all these years, with hon. members opposite looking for every possible ground of attack upon this government in view of the general election, with these hon. members running from one end of the country to the other-as was their right and duty-to arraign this government for its faults, when we find that, during all these years, no man ever raised the question, we have the most complete evidence that the action of the government of Canada was the action of the Canadian people as a whole.
The British government's next suggestion was for a fleet unit on the Pacific. Now it is important to emphasize the words ' on the Pacific '. In many cases-in most cases-when reference is made to. a_ fleet unit, these words ' on the Pacific ' are omitted. The suggestion was that a fleet unit should be established on the Pacific. Now, we are all proud of the great importance of our Pacific coast, yet it is the simple truth to say that the greater body of the Canadian people are tc be found nearer the Atlantic than to the Pacific. A naval policy which simply provided a fleet unit on the Pacific and ignored the Atlantic coast might be a policy to be talked of by the advocates in Downing street of a particular theory, but it is not a policy that could be presented in a manner acceptable to the Canadian people. If we were to 'sstablish a fleet unit on the Pacific, that would be followed, inevitably followed, by a fleet unit on the Atlantic, and the cost of these two fleet units would be enormous. I have not made up the figures, but I think it will be admitted that if we had undertaken to establish two fleet units, one on the Pacific, and one on the Atlantic, the cost would have been a great deal more than hon. gentlemen opposite would be disposed to approve. So, the idea of a fleet unit on the Pacific was not a practical one, it was not one that hon. members on the other side, I believe, would be prepared to adopt.
Thus, these two suggestions were, offered -first, a cash contribution, and second, a fleet unit on the Pacific. I have given the reasons which led our government to think that neither of these proposals could be accepted. The admiralty' had anticipated the possibility that we would not be able to agree with their views. They felt bound to present these views, but they had an intimation-not from us, but in the light of their own knowledge and experience-that these proposals might not be found satisfactory. A memorandum was prepared by the admiralty before the conference of 1909. It is well to observe that, though this appears in the records pf 1909,
it was prepared by the admiralty, in advance of the occasion.
It has, however, long been recognized that in defining the conditions under which the naval forces of the empire should be developed, other considerations than those of strategy alone must be taken into account. The various circumstances of the oversea dominions have to be borne in mind. Though all have in them the seeds of great advance m population, wealth and power, they have at the present time attained to different stages m their growth. Their geographical position lias subjected them to internal and external strains varying in kind and intensity. Iheir history and physical environment have given rise to individual national sentiment, for the expression of which room must be found. A simple contribution of money or material may be to one Dominion the most acceptable form in which to assist in imperial defence. Another, while ready to provide local naval forces, and to place them at the disposal of the Crown in the event of war, may wish to lay the foundations upon which a future navy of its own could be raised.
One might think that this was a memorandum prepared by the Canadian Minister of Militia, it reads so like an expression of Canadian opinion. I think it worth while, therefore, to call attention to the fact that this is the British admiralty memorandum:
A third may think that the best manner in which it can assist in promoting the interests of the empire is in undertaking certain local services not directly of a naval character, but which may relieve the imperial government from expenses which would otherwise fall on the British exchequer.
Canada did that. Canada undertook certain expenditures at Halifax and Esquimau, which largely relieved the British taxpayer from expenses which would otherwise have fallen upon them. '
If I may be permitted, I asked about that yesterday, but I have not received any satisfaction yet. Perhaps the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) would allow me to ask now: What were those expenses?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: What about your leader?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend says what about my leader. He had better say, what about the leaders of the lory party.
I sav that the right of any man m this country to declare his opinion in favour of independence is absolutely beyond question, and while I have no sympathy however with it, I would say without the slightest hesitation, that were we not allowed to express our opinions in this matter, we would be unworthy of our position as Canadian citizens. Why, Sir, is it forgotten-that a distinguished Canadian, a predecessor of my own in the office of the Minister of Finance, was so well known as an advocate of independence, that when, some years ago, the imperial authorities offered him imperial honours, he declined to accept those honours until he could make it clear that, in doing so, he would not cease to exercise his right to advocate, if ho wished, the independence of Canada? l will go further. I say that when a man wants to advocate in a constitutional way, that which I would hate, the annexation of this country to the United States, he has a perfect right to do it. And, in doing it he would not cease to exercise his freedom as a British subject.
Might I suggest that the difference is in legislating for independence rather than speaking for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There has been no proposal anywhere to legislate for independence nor do I expect that my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) will ever see such legislation proposed in the parliament of Canada. But I -was speaking of an extreme case, the extreme case of the advocate of annexation.
A great Englishman came over to Canada some years ago and settled in the city of Toronto. He is the one man whom I know in the Dominion of Canada who thinks that the manifest destiny of this Dominion is to become a portion of the American republic. I do not think I do him injustice when I state that he has long entertained that opinion. And those who know Goldwin Smith know that the thing he
thinks is the thing he will speak. But. though he entertains this opinion, he is recognized as one of the noblest citizens of Canada, and when, a few days ago, he was stricken with illness, a telegram came from King Edward to inquire about the health of his old friend, Goldwin Smith. This is the freest country in the world: let us see to it that we make no attempt to muzzle any one, who, in a constitutional way desires to speak the thought that is in him.
Though I mention these things, I have no sympathy with independence, and I would not think of sympathizing with a man who.advocates annexation. The point I want to make is that nothing is to be gained by attempting to muzzle the people of Canada and prevent them from advocating anything that, in their judgment, will make for the good of Canada.
We occasionally hear reference to South Africa and the dreadful things that happened in connection with the sending of the troops to that country. One would think that the South African war was the first one that had occurred to which the attention of the Canadian people had been drawn. It is not so. There was another war of considerable importance not many years ago. There came a moment when the heroic Gordon laid down his life and Khartoum fell. The heart of the empire was stirred; the heart of the whole British world was stirred. Australia felt the inspiration and thought that something might be done. And what of Canada? Did Canada move? It wTas not a Liberal government that was in power at that time, it was the Conservative government of Sir John Macdonald. And yet not a hand was lifted for the benefit of the empire, not a move was made. But individuals took action. General Laurie, a gallant Canadian, who represented my own constituency, and though one who differed from me in politics, always a good Canadian and a w'arm personal friend, went to Sir John Macdonald and said he would like to be instrumental in raising a force to go to the Sudan. Colonel Williams, a gallant Canadian who afterwards lost his life, tendered his services. What did the government do? Let them answer in their own words. On March 16, 1885, Mr. Blake asked the fol-< lowing question in this House
Whether any offer has been made by the government of Canada, or whether any offer has been made by any individual through the government of Canada, to equip and send a military contingent to the Soudan at the cost of Canada or of individual Canadians? Whether any offer of military assistance at the oost of the British government has been made by the government, or by individuals? Whether any reply has been received to any such offers? and wThether the correspondence will be laid on the table?
To these questions, Sir John Macdonald replied:

Secretary.
On February 13 following, Sir Saul Samuel, agent of New South Wales in London, wrote to the Secretary of State at the Colonial Office:
I have the honour to transmit for Lord Derby s information a further message in relation to the proposal of my government, in which it is stated that they will defray all expenses in connection with their offer.
Observe the difference. The New South Wales government tendered a force, and then, for fear there was any misunderstanding, they sent a message in which they said they would defray all expenses in connection with their offer. But when a telegram w'ent from the Canadian government, they took good care to make the matter so clear that there would be no mistake: Laurie, Williams and Melgund can all have a shy at it, bu't- not a penny out of the Canadian treasury. Let us see'how this occasion was treated in Australia. A despatch from Sydney, New South Wales, on the 3rd of March, 1885, had the following:
To-day was observed as a public holiday in celebration of the departure of the New South Wales contingent for the Soudan. The event is regarded as not only one of the greatest in the annals of the colonv, but as possessing a deep historic interest as the first occasion in which Australian troops have shared in the defence of the empire. From the date on which the colony's offer was accepted to the hour of the departure of the contingent public enthusiasm has been maintained at its utmost tension. The number of volunteers has reached six times the required strength of the force; and there lias been a continuous flow of contributions, in money mid in kind, from all quarters, and the latriotic fund now amounts to £45 000 The troops were reviewed on Saturdav by Lord

Augustus Loftus, Governor of New South Wales, in the presence of 50,000 spectators. On Sunday special services were held for the volunteers in the Anglican and Roman Catholic cathedrals, sermons being preached by the Primate and the Roman Catholic Archbishop.
To-day the streets forming the line of route from the barracks to the Circular quay, a distance of two miles, were lined by immense numbers of spectators, assembled from all parts, and forming a dense mass. The troops were escorted by 600 sailors and marines from the men-of-war stationed here, and by all the available local forces, and were accompanied by the Governor, the ministers, and the principal officials of the colony. The procession formed an imposing spectacle, and the popular enthusiasm was unbounded, the progress of the contingent being greeted with loud cheers and the frequent expression of good wishes from the assembled multitude.
That is what Australia did. Canada sent a message: 'Not a man, not a penny.' But there are other ways besides naval and military in which help may be given to the empire. Great Britain is in a much larger degree a nation of peace than she is a nation of war. She is a trading nation, and he who helps the trade of Great Britain is doing much to help the empire; that is what the Britisher thinks of it. Well, some years ago a good Conservative introduced a high tariff policy into this parliament, and among the criticisms of that measure in some quarters appeared the statement that a policy of that character designed to shut out British goods might tend to weaken British connection. Then the recognized organ of the Conservative party in the city of Toronto published in article in which it said that ' if this policy tended to weaken British connection, so much the worse for British connection.' That was the utterance of the recognized organ of the Conservative party at that time. Now, let us compare that with the Liberal record. This government had not been very long in office before it set itself to improve our commercial relations with Great Britain, and it brought down before this parliament what is known as the British pTeference. The Conservative government had put up the tariff in order to shut out British goods; this government endeavoured, so far as they could without damage to home industries, to give the British merchants a chance in Canada. And what then? Hon. gentlemen opposed the British preference from the beginning down to this moment.
No.

They wanted to say to John Bull: 'You cannot get a preference in this country unless you first give us one.' Where was their loyalty? He knows that in taking that step Canada led the way in which she has since been followed by New Zealand, in which she has been followed to a limited extent, and will be to a larger extent, by South Africa; he knows that_ the British preference brought down in this legislature many years ago has been regarded by every imperial statesman as a big contribution to imperial unity.

I have said, Sir, that Great Britain, as a trading nation, is more interested in the arts of peace than in the arts of war, and that the party or the government or the people who help to strengthen the trade relations with Great Britain are doing more for the empire than some others who are constantly shouting about loyalty. I noticed the other day in a Conservative paper a telegram from Montreal which mentions the name of an hon. gentleman who is not in the House at the present moment. The despatch reads:	-
Montreal. March 8, (Special).-Do away with the British preference and contribute $3,000,000 to the imperial navy is the policy advocated by Rudolphe Forget, M.P. for Char-

levoix, who left town this evening to give his vote on the navy Bill.
My hon. friend was rather more consistent on the question than some others have been. He certainly has not done much shouting about the British preference, and he would be in a better position to do away with it than some other gentlemen would be.
I noticed in connection with our German relations-and this is only an illustration for a minute-that a very estimable citizen of Toronto, whom we once had the honour of claiming as a fellow member of this House, my good friend, Mr. W. R. Brock, on the day it was announced that we had come to better trade relations with Germany, good strong Conservative that he was, announced that that arrangement was better than sending ten Dreadnoughts to Great Britain. If the re-establishing of friendly relations with Germany was better than sending ten Dreadnoughts to Britain, how many Dreadnoughts would measure the value that has been granted the empire by the British preference?
It was not a Liberal government which lagged behind in 1885; it was a Liberal government which did not lag behind, but which sent the troops to South Africa a few years ago, and we who know the whole history of that better than hon. gentlemen opposite, know how much the empire owes Sir Wilfrid Laurier in connection with that. It was a Liberal government that established the military college at Kingston; it is a Liberal government that will establish a naval college in Canada under this Bill. I have said, and I repeat that if you want to find the record of what has been done for the empire in Canada vou have to find it in the records of the Liberal party.
We are submitting this naval scheme to parliament with the firm conviction that it is a scheme which will deserve and receive the support of the Canadian people. It maintains the right of the Canadian government to control Canadian affairs in naval and military matters in time of peace. It provides the machinery whereby we may, in the event of war, instantly turn over that navy to more active service as a part of the imperial navy. We say we retain the right to deal with our own ships, and who else should have that Tight? We say that the scheme is in harmony with the wishes of the imperial authorities, although it does not go as far as they would desire, because the cost of what they would desire is beyond what we think is within the reasonable means of the Canadian people. It is in harmony with the best judgment of the House of Commons as expressed at a moment when it had withdrawn itself from partisanship, and was prepared to recognize its great responsibilities to the nation. Not only is it in harmony with the view of the Liberal party 2404
-I have no right, perhaps, my hon. friend the leader of the opposition may say it i3 presumption on my part to say what the Conservative party thought of it, but I will read from a Conservative authority, a high authority, a man who says that this policy is in harmony with all that is good for the Canadian people. and all that is desired by the British people. The quotation is not new, but there are some things that are good enough to bear repetition. I shall read from the remarks of Mr. A. W. Atwater, K.C., of Montreal, an ex-Conservative minister of the province of Quebec, who has recently returned from England. I am quoting from that good Conservative newspaper, the Montreal * Gazette ' and so there is no danger that the thing was turned the wrong way:
What the Englishman admires is a fellow who can stand up for himself, and what I found they admire in Canada is the effort she' is making to build up a fleet of her own. They admire and respect the capacity of Canada and any nation or dependency to look after itself. Hitherto there has been a patronizing air about the English with regard to Canada, because they knew that if we got into trouble they would have to look after us, but if Canada gets her own navy and can look after herself that will all change. The sooner we get our own navy the better-it is a necessity that must come, and there is no use delaying it. We must look after ourselves in a naval way just as we do in military matters. There is no doubt that is the feeling amongst the English people, and they regard it is a matter quite outside the domain of party politics, as it should be/
So, said Mr. A. W. Atwater, K.C., ex-provincial treasurer, who returned on Monday evening from a two months' stay in England, during which he witnessed the general elections, and had ample opportunity to gauge public feeling on this and other important matters.
The general opinion I got during my stay in England,' said Mr. Atwater, ' was that we should earn the respect of the people of the mother country more by showing our ability to defend ourselves than we could by any mere money contribution, unless it was to a very large amount and a permanent contribution. And that would not commend itself to many Canadians, nor could it be advocated by any party here. The opinion of all observers of imperial affairs was that they would have more respect for any portion of the empire which prepared to defend itself than for one which proposed to give a more or less-probably less-adequate sum toward the upkeep of the imperial navy.
' And with this I quite agree,' said Mr. Atwater. ' As a matter of keeping our own sqlf-respect, as well as the respect of the mother country, we should secure our own navy, and the sooner we get it in good working order the better. It will take a long time to do this, even with the assistance of England's enormous experience in naval affairs. And it seems to me that Canadians should join in this work irrespective of all party affiliations.

This naval project, said Mr. Atwater, was attracting much attention in England, and the people there were struck with the idea of the overseas dominions building ships and manning them with their own crews for imperial defence. In just the same way the mother country was deeply impressed with the manner in which Canada and the other Dominions sent their soldiers to fight in South Africa, where a mere money contribution would either have gone unnoticed, or been regarded as a pusillanimous manner of accepting the duty of defending the empire. Great Britain was very wealthy, and a contribution of even ten million pounds would be a mere matter of empire bookkeeping, and would not tend to reduce their taxation. But actual physical participation in the empire burden fired the British imagination, and excited their admiration.
Mr. Atwater properly called attention to the manner in which Canada responded to the need of the empire in South Africa. Then, as now, no doubt, there could have been found men, who would have said: ' Send over a few million dollars and put it in the hands of the Chancellor of the Exchequer.' Speaking from memory, we spent some two or three millions on that occasion. Now, suppose we had sent these two or three million dollars over, as the leader of the opposition proposes in the case of the navy, and dumped it into the imperial treasury, we might have got a vote of thanks for it in some way, but would it have made any lasting impression? On the contrary, it is an instrument drawing us closer to the' empire. Every step we take in military affairs is taken in co-operation with and under the advice of the highest imperial officers. As it has been with the army, so it will be with the navy. Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair I desire to submit to the House a matter which has been before the Public Accounts Committee, and which, I think, demands the very serious consideration of this House, inasmuch as it involves, if I may be permitted to use the language of a Sabbath editorial of the Toronto 'Globe' in this connection, ' not only the methods but the honour' of the chief spending department of this government. I refer to the purchase of the property at Richibucto, N. B., which is known as 'the saw-dust wharf' and so described in the Auditor General's Report. Briefly, the department bought this property from one Thomas O. Murray on the eve of the last general election, and paid $5,000 for it; Mr. Murray bought the property for the purpose of selling it to the department and paid $700 for it; so the department paid Mr. Murray over seven times the price which Mr. Murray paid for the property; in other words, the department provided Mr. Murray with a rake-off or a profit of $4,300 upon a seven hundred dollar investment.
Nowu Mr. Speaker, if nothing more were to be said in connection with this case than the simple statement of this indisputable fact, it is enough to condemn the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley). But the matter assumes a far more serious aspect when we consider the character of the property, the conditions which exist at Richibucto, the history of the transaction from the beginning down to the registration of the deed by which the title of the property is vested in the Crown, the conduct of the Minister of Public Works after the matter became a public scandal and the unprecedented defence which he assayed to make of the transaction before the Public Accounts Committee. These considerations present a train of circumstances which establish beyond doubt | that th'e transaction was a positive

fraud, deliberately planned from, the beginning for a corrupt purpose, and make it impossible to acquit the responsible minister of the department of complicity in it. Indeed, there is evidence which indicates that the Minister of Public Works was the originator of the transaction.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman is going beyond the bounds of parliamentary usage when he states that a letter written by the Minister of Public Works shows insincerity. Insincerity cannot be attributed to any member of parliament.

It must be borne in mind that I am discussing a report of the Public Accounts Committee, the evidence of which is for the consideration of every member of this House. The issue in this case is whether this was a bona fide transaction. I have already said that there is evidence which indicates that the minister was cognizant of this transaction from the very beginning, and that the transaction was put through for corrupt purposes. I am discussing the question with reference to that issue, and surely it is competent for me and for this House to discuss the evidence which is reported for the consideration of the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is competent to bring that evidence before the House, and it is competent for the hon. gentleman to discuss that evidence, but when it is brought up in this way, I do not think the hon. gentleman is at_ liberty to attribute wrong-doing to a minister or to any member of parliament. If he desires to lav charges, the method of laying those charges is known to him. But I do not think he is at liberty in this debate to attribute w'rong-doing to any member of the House.

I certainly bow to your ruling. But this is a case which does not arise in the usual way, because it is a case that has already been fully investigated, and we are discussing the evidence. It is not a question of making a charge, it is a question of dealing with a transaction which has been investigated by a committee of this House, and which has been sent to this House for its judgment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I will read these words from May:
For the same reason no charge of a personal character can be raised save upon a direct and substantive motion to that effect.

There is this to be said about it. Suppose a witness gave evidence before the Committee on Public Accounts of a corrupt transaction, would a member discussing that evidence in this House, be bound to say that he did not believe that witness? Could he not argue that the evidence of that witness was supported? Suppose there were two witnesses, suppose there were half a dozen witnesses, suppose their testimony was corroborated by a written document, would any member, in discussing that, be obliged to

speak as if there was no written document and no corroborative evidence? I do not think, with all deference, the rule could possibly apply to a case where the evidence has been taken and where that evidence is being discussed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question is doubtless complicated. But at the same time I think that the hon. gentleman partly brings the trouble upon himself by the moment and the manner he has chosen to discuss it. The rule does seem clear, that if a charge of wrong-doing is to be made against a minister or any member of the House, it should be done by a substantive motion. The hon. gentleman has not taken that method. I think he is at liberty to discuss the evidence and to lay that evidence before the House; I am not clear that he is at liberty to make a charge of wrong-doing against a minister of the Crown or against a member 'of the House without a substantive motion. The rules of order governing all debates are not suspended for this debate.

I am not making a charge, I am considering a matter which has already been fully investigated. If I made a charge in this matter I would simply be required to say that I, as a member of this House, am informed and believe that such and such a thing is true, then that would be referred to a committee of the House. I think this House has now upon its records a report from one of its committees which indicates that this is a corrupt transaction, and that the Minister of Public Works was involved in it from the beginning.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have quoted 'the hon. gentleman the authority under which I am acting. If the hon. gentleman has any contrary authorities I would be willing to hear them.

Would you allow me to say one word? The hon. member charges that the Minister of Public Works is involved in this corrupt transaction from the beginning. The charge which the hon. member has -presented to the House by way of an amendment is a motion of want of confidence, he makes no stated charge against me. The hon. gentleman has not the courage to make a charge against me.
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) is raising a point of order, he is at liberty to discuss that point of order. But he is not at liberty to address the House on any other matter.

Referring to the point of order, the hon. member was discussing the question and dealing with the evidence before the House, simply stating that the evidence indicates so and so. That is all, and to my mind he is quite within his rights in saying so. That is all he said, and I respectfully submit that that is not outside the common amenities of debate in this House in dealing with a question of that nature when the evidence is before the House for consideration.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think in a matter of this kind I should not interpret the rule very broadly. I am inclined to interpret the rule broadly as far as liberty of debate goes on questions of debate generally, but where a question of personal character or wrong-doing or a charge of

that nature comes up in regard to a member, I think I should interpret the rule rather more stringently, and ask the hon. gentleman to comply closely with it. In that case, while I am perfectly willing that the hon. gentleman should lay the evidence before the House, I still think that if he wishes to proceed as far as laying a charge against the minister of insincerity or wrong-doing, he should proceed in the way indicated, by a specific motion.

I bow to your ruling. My statement was that the evidence that has been submitted to this House from the Public Accounts Committee proves, and to my mind, proves beyond a doubt that this transaction was a corrupt and fraudulent transaction, and I said furthermore that there was evidence and much evidence to indicate that the Minister of Public Works was cognizant of it from the beginning. That was the question I was discussing.

Now I regret that I Lave occupied so much time of the House. But this has impressed me as a matter of serious importance, not because of the amount of money involved, which is comparatively small, but because it involves as I have said, and as the Toronto ' Globe ' has said, not only the methods, but the honour of the chief spending department of this government. For that reason I have thought it my duty to put upon record, not my statement or interpretation of the evidence, but the evidence just as it was given, so that members of the House may see for themselves, and draw their own conclusions. There is one other matter I want to refer to. In addition to Mr. Loggie there was another witness produced, Mr. J. D. Irvine. He was not called by myself, he was called by my hon. friend from Carleton who was defending this transaction before the Public Acoounts Committee, as he has been called upon to defend so many transactions of the Public Works Department in that committee, and he is deserving of the sympathy of the House in that connection. Now, Mr. Irving was asked as to the valuation, and I will quote from his evidence a line or two page 129:
Q. Suppose that you were in business in Richibucto as Messrs. Loggie are, and you owned that property, what would you sell it for?-A. Well, I do not know if I had it that I would sell it at all, unless I could get another one to replace it.
Q. It has been stated by Mr. Stead in that letter which he wrote, to me in answer to that request for information in regard to the knowledge which he had before reporting on the value of this proprty, that there was a party in Buctouche who said that he would not take $10,000 for it if he owned it, and he said, you are the gentleman to whom he referred. Did you tell Mr. Stead that?-A. Well, I did, I said that if I had it in the town of Buctouche, situated as it was there, I would not take it.
Further on:	[DOT]
Q. If you owned that property in Richibucto, would you take $5,000 for it?-A. No, Sir,
I would not, not by any means.
That was the evidence given to the Minister of Public Works. But in cross examination it turned out that J. D. Irving was, like Mr. Loggie, a gentleman who had been drawing large sums of money from the Public Works Department upon the certificate of Geoffrey Stead. He had a scow down there, of which he dared not place the valuation at over $150, for which he had received about $6(10 rent from the Public

Works Department. Here is more of Mr. Irving's evidence in his cross-examination, page 130:
Q. You spoke about having some wharf property yourself at Buctouche?-A. Yes.
Q. I think you said you had about half a mile?-A. In the vicinity of the water front.
Q. How much did you pay for your wharf property in Buctouche?-A. One wharf I bought for $220, somewhere about ten or fifteen years ago, I could not tell exactly.
Q. And you have a half a mile of it on the shore?-A. I have close on to half a mile, 1 think.
This gentleman who said that if he had this property in Buctouche he would "not sell it for $10,000, had actually bought his own wharf at Buctouche with half a mile of shore for $220.
Which, at page 134, he says is yielding $500 a year income.

That is the evidence that we have adduced before the Public Accounts Committee in support of 'this valuation, the evidence of A. & R. Loggie and J. D. Irving. I think if that evidence has any effect it is only to confirm the abundance of evidence which this record contains that this transaction is, as I said at the outset, a positive fraud, deliberately planned from the beginning, and I say to the Minister of Public Works that if this evidence does not convict him of complicity in this transaction it certainly involves him in the gravest _ suspicion that has ever surrounded a minister of the cabinet with reference to a transaction of this kind. I think the evidence I have quoted establishes what I have said. I, therefore, beg to move:
That all the words after the word ' that ' to the end of the motion be left out and the following substituted therefor:-
The evidence taken before the Public Accounts Committee and submitted to this House touching a payment of $5,000 to T. O. Murray in connection with the purchase by the Public Works Department of the sawdust wharf at Richibucto, New Brunswick, as set out at page V-188 of the Auditor General's Report for the year ending March 31, 1909, discloses that said purchase was a corrupt and fraudulent transaction which deserves the severest condemnation of the House.

Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
Shall we go on with this debate to-morrow?
